400.title: The person; the gods enter through the doors of the body (1.2)
400.hook: the gods are offered a cow, then a horse, as a home, and turn both down. then they see a human being
400.tomorrow: hunger and thirst ask for a place
400.howItsDone: In Vedic and later Hindu ritual, the body's senses are linked to deities, and some rites include touching the limbs while reciting mantras, a practice called nyasa, which echoes the idea of the gods dwelling in the body.

segments.voice: Yesterday: atma, the self alone, which looked and said, let me create worlds. Your line was the worlds.

The worlds are made, and the Aitareya has a house-hunting story. The self shapes a cosmic person and draws the great powers out of it: fire, wind, the sun, the moon. Gods. But the gods have nowhere to live. They're adrift, the text says, fallen into a great ocean, and they come back asking for a home. So the self brings them a cow. The gods look it over: no, this isn't enough for us. It brings them a horse. Not enough either. Then it brings them a human being.
screen: `THE GODS HAVE NOWHERE TO LIVE.` → `A COW? NOT ENOUGH.` → `A HORSE? NOT ENOUGH.` → `THEN, A PERSON.`

segments.voice: When the gods see the person, purusha, they say: sukritam bata. Well made, indeed! The person is truly well made, the text adds. That's the Upanishad's verdict on the human body. Not a prison. Not a burden. A good piece of work, the house the gods accepted. Then the self says: enter, each into your own place. And no god just walks in. Each one changes shape to fit. Fire becomes speech, and enters the mouth. Wind becomes breath, and enters the nostrils. The sun becomes sight, and enters the eyes. The directions of space become hearing, and enter the ears. Plants and trees become the hairs, and enter the skin. The moon becomes mind, and enters the heart. Death becomes the down-going breath, and enters the navel. The waters become seed, and enter the organ of generation. Read that list slowly and the body looks different. On this map, when you talk, there's fire in your mouth. When you look up, the sun is looking out through you. Your quiet, changeable mind is the moon. Even death has a room in the house, low down, at the navel, doing its work. The Upanishad isn't asking you to worship your eyes. It's saying the great powers out there and the small doors in here belong to one system, and the person is where they meet. Perhaps that's why a cow wasn't enough, and a horse wasn't enough. They needed a place where speech, sight, mind and the rest could all live together.

segments.voice: Bring attention to your closed mouth, where the story puts fire as speech, then to the breath in the nostrils, the wind, and to the eyes, the sun. Move on to the ears and the directions, the skin and the plants and trees, the heart and the moon as mind. Then rest in the whole house at once, every door open.
The person. Purusha, the human being the gods called well made, the one house where fire, wind, sun and moon could each find their door.
Your line: the gods within. Tomorrow, two more guests knock at the door. Four hundred days, done.

401.title: Hunger and thirst ask for a place (1.2)
401.hook: once the gods have moved in, two more voices speak up: hunger and thirst want a home too
401.tomorrow: the self enters through the crown of the head
401.howItsDone: Teachers of the Aitareya read this passage when explaining why appetite goes with every sense, and in Vedic ritual each offering is made to a particular deity, the share the passage says hunger and thirst join.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the person, the house the gods called well made, with fire in the mouth and the moon in the heart. Your line was the gods within.

Everyone's moved in. Fire has the mouth, the sun has the eyes, the moon has the heart. The house is full and humming. Then there's a knock. Two figures stand outside, and they were there before the gods arrived. In fact, they're why the gods went house-hunting at all. Their names are hunger and thirst, ashanaya and pipasa, and they say to the self: what about us? Find us a place too. You know these two: mid-afternoon, midnight at the fridge, long meetings. The Aitareya gives them a whole verse.
screen: `THE HOUSE IS FULL.` → `A KNOCK AT THE DOOR.` → `HUNGER AND THIRST: WHAT ABOUT US?`

segments.voice: Here's the order in the story. When the gods first fell into the great ocean, the self touched that whole creation with hunger and thirst. That's why the gods asked for a home: they wanted a place to eat. So hunger and thirst are older than the house. They didn't break in. They were part of the plan. Now, with the gods settled, the two ask: find a place for us. The self doesn't banish them, or scold them as enemies of the spirit. It says, more or less: I'll give you a share among these gods. You'll be partners with them. That's why, the text explains, whenever an offering is made to any god, hunger and thirst share in it. An ordinary arrangement, and a generous one. One way to hear it: when your eyes see, they get hungry for more seeing. When your ears hear a song, they want the next one. When the mind, the moon in the heart, settles on an idea, it gets thirsty for another. On this reading, every power comes with an appetite. Some later teachers read the passage as a sober account of the human condition: wanting runs through every sense. But the story itself is calm about it. Nobody is shamed for being hungry. The self knows who lives in the house, and gives each one its share.

402.title: The self enters through the crown of the head (1.3)
402.hook: the house is full of gods, and the self asks a strange question: if all of them do all the work, then who am I?
402.howItsDone: Some Hindu men, especially in priestly families, keep a tuft of hair, the shikha, near the crown, and some yoga and meditation teachers direct attention to the crown of the head, which later texts call the brahmarandhra.

segments.voice: Yesterday: appetite, hunger and thirst, given no room of their own but a share in every god's offering. Your line was they too need a home.

Here's a company where every department runs perfectly. Speech does the talking. Breath does the breathing. The eyes see, the ears hear, the mind thinks. Then the founder walks through the building with an uncomfortable thought: if they all do everything, what am I for? That's where the Aitareya's first chapter ends. The self has made worlds, a person, a house full of gods and appetites. Now it looks at all that working machinery and asks how it could possibly be there without itself.
screen: `EVERY DEPARTMENT RUNS ITSELF.` → `WHAT AM I FOR?` → `THE SELF ASKS THE SAME.`

segments.voice: The text gives the self two questions. How could this be without me? And: by which way shall I enter? Then comes a list, almost comic. If speaking is done by speech, breathing by breath, seeing by the eye, hearing by the ear, touching by the skin, thinking by the mind, then who am I? So the self finds its own door. Not the mouth, the nostrils or the eyes; those were taken. It splits open the seam at the very top of the skull, where the bones meet, and enters there. The text names that door vidriti, the cleft, and calls it the place of joy. Every other god came in through a working opening. The self comes in through a door that does nothing at all. It doesn't speak, see or breathe. It's just the way in. Then the text says the self has three dwelling places, three states of dream: this is a dwelling, this is a dwelling, this is a dwelling. Commentators argue over which three. Once inside, the self looks around, wondering: is there anything here that could speak of something other than me? And it sees this very person as Brahman, spread out everywhere. Idam adarsham, it says. I have seen this. Later yoga traditions talk about a point at the crown called the brahmarandhra, and some readers connect it to this passage. The Aitareya itself just says: there's a door at the top, and that's where the one who sees came in.

segments.voice: Sit tall and let your attention rest on the crown of your head, where the seams of the skull meet: air, warmth, the weight of your hair, or nothing much. This spot isn't talking or watching or breathing, and still something is aware of it. Rest in that awareness, the one that came in by the quiet door.

403.title: The three births — conception, birth, and death as birth (2.1)
403.hook: the Aitareya counts a person's births, and gets to three, and the third one is what most people would call dying
403.howItsDone: Hindu life-cycle rites, the samskaras, mark stages from before birth through death, and the funeral rites (antyeshti) and later shraddha offerings are understood by many families as sending the departed on to their next life.

segments.voice: Yesterday: vidriti, the door at the top of the head, where the self came in and said, I have seen this.

How many birthdays do you have? One, obviously. It's on your ID. Ask a family and it gets fuzzier. There's the day you were born. There's the day, months before, when someone found out you were coming. And in some families there's a day after the person is gone, when the family gathers and the rites send them on. The Aitareya's second chapter counts births too. It counts three, and it puts them somewhere you might not expect.
screen: `HOW MANY BIRTHDAYS DO YOU HAVE?` → `THE DAY SOMEONE FOUND OUT.` → `THE AITAREYA COUNTS THREE.`

segments.voice: The first birth, the text says, happens in the father. The seed is the strength gathered from all his limbs, a self carried in himself. When he places it in the mother, that's the first birth. Then the second. The child becomes one with the mother, like a part of her own body, and so, the text says, she doesn't harm it. She nourishes this self inside her, and so she is to be nourished in turn. The father cares for the child before birth and after, and in caring for the child, the text says, he cares for himself, for so the line goes on and the worlds continue. The child's arrival is the second birth. Then the third. The child grows and takes the parent's place, carrying on the good work. And the parent, having done what there was to do, grows old, and departs. And departing, the text says, he is born again. That's the third birth. Death isn't the opposite of birth here. It's the next one. Then the chapter turns to a seer. It quotes a verse from the Rig Veda in the voice of the sage Vamadeva: while still in the womb, I knew all the births of the gods. A hundred iron fortresses held me down, and like a hawk I broke out. Knowing this, the text says, Vamadeva rose up from the body and reached immortality. Notice what it honors along the way: the mother is to be nourished. Even in a list of births, it stops to say who needs care.

segments.voice: Let one breath go to the people who carried you before you were born, whoever held the hope of you, and one to those who fed and held you before you could thank them. Then, gently, think of someone who has died; in the Aitareya's count, that was a birth too. Let a breath go to them, wherever they are.

Vamadeva, the seer who said, while still in the womb, I knew all the births of the gods. The Aitareya counts three births: conception in the father, birth from the mother, and death, when a person departs and is born again.

404.title: "Consciousness is Brahman" — prajnanam brahma (3.1)
404.hook: the Aitareya ends by asking which one is the self, and answers with two words that became one of the great sayings
404.tomorrow: six students, one year of practice before asking
404.howItsDone: In the Advaita tradition, the four great sayings are taught to students and to those taking monastic vows, and prajnanam brahma is the one associated with the Rig Veda; teachers in other Vedanta schools comment on the same line differently.

segments.voice: Yesterday: three births, in the father, from the mother, and in departing, and Vamadeva breaking out like a hawk. Today, the Aitareya's last chapter.

Point at yourself. Where did your finger go? Probably the chest, maybe the face. Now ask: is that me, or is that where I keep the thing that's me? It's a children's puzzle, and a very old one. The Aitareya saves it for its last chapter. After the worlds, the gods moving in, hunger and thirst, the door at the crown and the three births, it stops telling stories and asks straight out: who is this one we call the self? And it ends with two words.
screen: `POINT AT YOURSELF.` → `IS THAT ME?` → `WHICH ONE IS THE SELF?`

segments.voice: First the question: is the self the one by which we see? By which we hear, smell, speak, taste? Then the text looks at the heart and mind and lists what they do. Awareness. Perception. Discernment. Intelligence. Wisdom. Insight. Steadiness. Thought. Reflection. Drive. Memory. Intention. Purpose. Life. Desire. Will. All of these, it says, are only names of prajnana. Prajnana means knowing, awareness, consciousness: pra, forth or fully, and jnana, knowing. Then the list widens. This is Brahman. This is Indra, and Prajapati, and all the gods. The five elements, earth, wind, space, water and fire. Every creature, born from an egg, a womb, moisture or a sprout. Horses, cows, people, elephants, whatever breathes, walks, flies or stands still. All of it is guided by consciousness, rests on consciousness. The world has consciousness for its eye. And then: prajnanam brahma. Consciousness is Brahman. Many Hindu teachers in the Advaita tradition count this among four mahavakyas, great sayings, one from each Veda. This is the Rig Veda's. You've already heard the other three this year: tat tvam asi in the Chandogya, and aham brahma asmi and ayam atma brahma in the Brihadaranyaka. Schools read the saying differently. Advaita hears a strict identity: awareness and Brahman are one. Other Vedanta schools hear Brahman as the conscious ground all knowing depends on, while keeping a distinction between the soul and God. Either way, the text points somewhere specific: not at the finger, but at what's aware of it.

405.title: Six students, one year of practice before asking (1.1)
405.hook: six seekers arrive at a sage's door with their questions ready, and he tells them to wait a year
405.tomorrow: Q1: where do creatures come from?
405.howItsDone: In traditional Hindu learning, a student lives with or near the teacher and studies for long periods before being taught the deepest texts; some Vedanta teachers today still ask students to study and practice before taking up the Upanishads.

segments.voice: Yesterday: prajnana. Prajnanam brahma, consciousness is Brahman, the great saying that closed the Aitareya. Today, a new Upanishad, and six people with questions.

You've finally got a meeting with the expert. You walk in with your list of questions, and before you can open your mouth, they say: come back in a year. The Prashna Upanishad opens with six serious people who come to a great teacher, wood for his fire in their hands, and that is roughly what he tells them. Prashna means question. The whole Upanishad is built from the questions they ask. But first, they have to wait.
screen: `YOUR LIST OF QUESTIONS, READY.` → `COME BACK IN A YEAR.` → `PRASHNA MEANS QUESTION.`

segments.voice: Tradition places the Prashna in the Atharva Veda. It names its six students one by one: Sukesha Bharadvaja. Satyakama Shaibya. Gargya Sauryayani. Kausalya Ashvalayana. Bhargava of Vidarbha. And Kabandhi Katyayana. They were devoted to Brahman, the text says, grounded in it, seeking the highest. And they came to the sage Pippalada, fuel in hand, sure he could tell them everything. Pippalada says: stay one more year, with tapas, with brahmacharya, and with shraddha. Discipline, a disciplined life of study, and faith. Then ask whatever you like. And then the line that makes this teacher worth listening to: if we know, we'll tell you all of it. If we know. A great sage, six eager students, and he doesn't promise answers. He promises honesty. Think about what the year does. A question asked the day it occurs to you is often a reflex. A question carried for a year, through practice and ordinary days, has had time to become real. Some answer themselves. Some change shape. The ones still standing are worth a teacher's time. And notice what he asks for. Not cleverness. Not money. Discipline, a steady life, and trust. In the coming days, each student asks one question. The first five: where creatures come from, which powers hold up the body, where breath comes from, what's awake in sleep, and what happens to the one who meditates on om.

406.title: Q1: where do creatures come from? matter and breath (1)
406.hook: the first student asks where living things come from, and Pippalada answers with a pair: matter and breath, moon and sun
406.carry: the two paths of the sun
406.tomorrow: Q2: which gods hold the body?
406.howItsDone: Many Hindus mark the sun's northward turn at Makar Sankranti in mid-January and treat the northern half of the year, uttarayana, as an auspicious time, an idea that echoes the two paths of texts like this one.

segments.voice: Yesterday: six students, told to wait a year before asking. Your line was earn the question. Now the year is up.

The six students have kept the discipline. The first to step forward is Kabandhi Katyayana, with a question as old as asking: sir, from where are these creatures born? Children ask some version of it. Where did I come from? Where did the dog come from, the ants, the trees? A biologist would answer one way, a grandmother another. Pippalada answers with a story, and at its center is a pair, two things that need each other, the way a song needs both silence and sound.
screen: `THE YEAR IS UP.` → `SIR, WHERE DO CREATURES COME FROM?` → `THE ANSWER IS A PAIR.`

segments.voice: Pippalada says: Prajapati, the lord of creatures, wanted offspring. He did tapas, the inner heat you met with Bhrigu, and from that heat he produced a pair: rayi and prana. Rayi means wealth, substance, matter: the stuff that takes form. Prana is breath, life, the energy that moves it. These two together, he thought, will make creatures for me. Then the pair shows up everywhere. The sun is prana. The moon is rayi. In a month, the dark half belongs to rayi, the bright half to prana. In a day, night is rayi, day is prana. Food, too, is Prajapati, because from food comes the seed from which creatures are born. Matter and life, always in pairs. Then the answer turns to people. The year itself is Prajapati, and it has two paths, a southern and a northern. Those who honor sacrifice and good works, digging wells, giving, keeping the rites, take the southern path, the path of the ancestors, to the world of the moon. And from there they return. Those who seek the self through tapas, a disciplined life, faith and knowledge take the northern path, to the sun. That, the text says, is the resting place of breath, the immortal, the fearless. From there they do not return. So where do creatures come from? From matter meeting breath. And where do they go? The text names two paths, and what sets a person on either one is how they live.
screen: `PRAJAPATI'S TAPAS MAKES A PAIR.` · `RAYI IS MATTER; PRANA IS BREATH.` · `THE MOON AND THE SUN.` · `TWO PATHS: SOUTHERN AND NORTHERN.` · then, large: `RAYI AND PRANA.`

segments.voice: Feel the body's weight, the bones and muscle, the pressure where you touch the chair or floor: that's rayi, matter, the moon side. Then feel the breath moving through it, warming and lifting it: that's prana, the sun side. Rest on both at once, the stillness that holds and the motion that lives; neither one is enough alone.
Rayi, wealth and matter, paired with prana, breath. Where do creatures come from? From rayi and prana, the moon and the sun, which Prajapati made as a pair.

Your line: the two paths of the sun. That's week fifty-eight: the person, hunger and thirst, the door at the top, three births, the great saying, six students, and matter and breath. Day four hundred six.
